title: Give the model the role and the reader
body: Say who it is writing as and for whom (e.g. 'a CFO who skims'). Output changes more from audience than from adjectives.

title: Paste the source, don't describe it
body: Paste call notes, docs or logs. Summaries of summaries lose the details that matter.

title: Ask it to flag gaps instead of guessing
body: Add 'If the input doesn't support an answer, write NEEDS REVIEW.' This cuts made-up details in customer-facing work.

title: Use structure for reusable outputs
body: Request fixed sections or a table so status updates and POC docs look the same every week.

title: Iterate in two passes
body: First ask for a draft, then ask it to critique the draft as the skeptical buyer, then revise.

title: Keep a personal prompt library
body: Save prompts that worked with your [BRACKET] variables. Our prompts page is a starting point.

title: Check your company's data policy first
body: Don't paste customer data, credentials or contracts into tools your company hasn't approved.

title: Verify every number and claim
body: Treat model output as a draft. Check figures, product capabilities and competitor claims before they reach a customer.

title: Use AI for demo data, not demo truth
body: Generate fake but realistic sample data; never let the model invent features your product doesn't have.

title: Turn tribal knowledge into runbooks
body: Paste Slack threads and ask for numbered steps with verification and rollback. Then test the runbook once yourself.

title: Prep with a role-play
body: Ask the model to play the skeptical buyer or security reviewer and run through your demo or answers.

title: Learn how your tools connect to AI
body: Standards like the Model Context Protocol let assistants reach your tools and data; understanding them is quickly becoming part of deployment work.
